title: Low-resource language AI adoption
description: For a district or state champion bringing a tribal or low-resource language onto India’s language AI infrastructure. Built on the Pathway Model: where it applies, what it enables, the jobs to do, insights across them, and how proven it is.

purpose.label: What it is for
purpose.value: To help a state, district, university or NGO that already has local administrative backing bring a low-resource or tribal language onto India’s language AI infrastructure, drawing on the experience of bringing Bhili to the AI map in Nandurbar.

purpose.label: The problem
purpose.value: Government services, health information, agricultural advisories, legal aid and education platforms are built mostly for the dominant scheduled languages, so tribal and indigenous communities are effectively excluded from digital governance. Infrastructure gets built where training data exists, and data gets built where communities are literate, connected and economically active, so the gap persists. There is no commercial case for a private developer to close it.

purpose.label: Why voice AI
purpose.value: Speech needs no literacy, device fluency or familiarity with administrative language. A citizen who cannot write her name can still describe a problem and understand a response, if the service speaks her language.

purpose.label: Use cases
items: A crop advisory line or agricultural IVR, queried by voice with a voice reply in the same language
A frontline health worker’s tool, for example an ASHA worker explaining a protocol
A government helpline
A first keyword-spotting model for 20–30 priority terms, such as health service names, scheme names, crop names or emergency phrases

purpose.label: Who benefits
purpose.value: The farmer, the frontline health worker, the elder or low-literacy citizen, and the contributors who are paid for recording.

purpose.label: Who it is for
purpose.value: A District Collector, a Secretary, or a program lead at an institution that has decided to champion a language: capable people who are short on time.

context.label: Sector
context.value: Public services: government schemes, health information, agricultural advisories, legal aid and education.

context.label: People served
context.value: Tribal and indigenous language communities excluded from digital governance, especially women, elders and low-literacy citizens.

context.label: Geography
context.value: India. The reference is Bhili in Nandurbar, Maharashtra. The language has no standard script of its own.

context.label: Organisational capacity
context.value: Local administrative backing already in place; a champion who meets four criteria; an institutional anchor committed for 2–3 years; a full-time Nodal Officer.

context.label: Existing infrastructure
context.value: India’s language AI infrastructure: Bhashini, ULCA, AI4Bharat’s tools, State Data Centres. A real government service that can deploy the outcome.

context.label: Regulatory environment
context.value: Consent and data-protection compliance under the DPDP Act. Open release under CC BY 4.0 or equivalent.

context.label: Scale
context.value: Reference language with a 10–20 lakh speaker base and no production-grade dataset. Cost rises as speakers fall and falls as they rise.

context.label: Resources
context.value: ₹84 lakh to ₹1 crore for foundation-building. Data collection of 9+ months under normal conditions.

based_on.label: Adoptions drawn on
items: Project Astitva, Bhili, Nandurbar (Maharashtra): the reference implementation, with the District Collector as champion, Karya for data collection and AI4Bharat as technical partner.
Mission BAANI, Assam: named as a source. No detail on its language, approach or results is given.

based_on.label: Deployment reference
based_on.value: MahaVISTAAR and POCRA (Maharashtra State Agriculture Department), the live service used as the reference for an application owner.

based_on.label: Methodology
based_on.value: AI4Bharat’s published methodology, which the timeline steps and data volume tiers follow.

based_on.label: Convenings
based_on.value: A workshop for District Collectors (MahaPMU) and several convenings with people and institutions working on low-resource languages.

based_on.label: DC meeting checklist
based_on.value: The MahaPMU checklist: the stage sequence and timings, each job’s checklist items, and the PMU role tags.

based_on.label: Not recorded

outcomes: People who speak the language can use government services by voice in their own language, without needing to read, type or use the administrative language.
A public language dataset and model that other researchers, departments and states can build on without renegotiating access.
Paid work for contributors from the language community, with the money staying in the district.
Each recording session also preserves spoken knowledge held by elderly speakers, although livelihood motivates participation more than preservation does.
Reported results from a completed run: not stated. The milestones in the Sequence tab are targets.
insights: The champion convenes, funds and provides continuity, and experts make the domain decisions: script, dialect, quality thresholds and model architecture. The champion’s role is closer to a midwife’s than an owner’s: facilitate, then step back.
The community is the centre of the effort, not a stakeholder at the edge. Livelihood and seeing real results in their own language motivate more than a preservation appeal.

Real use is the test. A model that performs well in controlled conditions can still underperform on real dialects and noise, so field testing and acceptance by the deploying department stay part of the process.

The project should not depend on any one person. A Nodal Officer appointed to a post, and a formal written order issued by the champion, let it continue through a transfer: a written order survives a change in priorities, and a verbal agreement rarely does.

roles.name: Champion
roles.description: Convenes, funds and provides continuity, enabling decisions rather than making them. Meets four criteria: alignment of care, direct influence, power to convene and mobilise resources, and local community respect.
roles.example: E.g. a District Collector, the Secretary of the Department of Tribal Affairs, a Chief Secretary or an Agriculture Secretary.

roles.name: Nodal Officer
roles.description: Leads the PMU and coordinates the effort day to day. Appointed to a post, not a person, so the project survives a transfer. A full-time officer is assumed.

roles.name: Steering Committee
roles.description: Cross-department authority. Approves budget and direction. Reviews quarterly. In the checklist it also reviews vendor proposals on cost items, and the vendor’s work plan before the language survey starts.

roles.name: Project Management Unit (PMU)
roles.description: The Nodal Officer’s team of execution. Coordinates the work day to day, gathers existing community resources, drafts the scope document with the Ecosystem Orchestrator, runs the weekly review and coordinates vendors once contracted. Two arms kept independent of each other. Management arm: procurement, vendor management, reporting. Quality arm: validation standards, sign-off. The checklist calls the Quality arm “Quality PMU”.

roles.name: District / Local Administration
roles.description: Convenes, funds and champions the effort.

roles.name: District-Level Line Departments
roles.description: Hold the ground and provide continuity between phases.

roles.name: Line Secretary
roles.description: Reviews monthly: progress, outcomes and priorities across all district language projects.

roles.name: Core Application Owner
roles.description: Deploys the outcome through a real, live service. Owns fine-tuning and upkeep.

roles.name: Ecosystem Orchestrator
roles.description: Leads orchestration across the whole ecosystem. A neutral party with no vendor stake. Also called the orchestrating partner.
roles.example: E.g. PxD or an EkStep Foundation equivalent.
roles.see: In the DC checklist, PxD acts as the Ecosystem Orchestrator, so its items count as PMU’s.

roles.name: Central Program Office
roles.description: Sets the transcription guidelines, metadata schema and quality bar, applied uniformly across every field team.

roles.name: Linguistic Expert
roles.description: Validates content and resolves dialect and language questions. With community members, decides script and dialect.

roles.name: Community Heads
roles.description: Local community heads and influencing members. Legitimise the effort and mobilise participation. The centre of the ecosystem, not a stakeholder at the edge.

roles.name: Community Contributors
roles.description: Create, validate and own the language. Includes Audio Contributors, who record the raw data, and Voice Artists, who record professional-quality voice in studio settings.
roles.example: Use any community-led radio station if one exists.

roles.name: Data Collection Agency
roles.description: Field data collection, transcription, platform and task management, first-pass validation. Final validation sign-off and model building are out of scope.
roles.example: E.g. Karya, JoshTalks, Shoonya-integrated vendors, BhashaDaan (volunteer channel).

roles.name: Technical Partner
roles.description: Trains, benchmarks and maintains the models, including retraining cycles, and reports collection misses. Also called the Technical / Model-Building Partner or Model Builder. Field collection, community convening and deployment ownership are out of scope.

roles.name: Model Hoster
roles.description: Sovereign, publicly accessible hosting, with API and service availability. Also called the Model Hosting Platform. Model quality decisions, data collection and annotation are out of scope.

roles.name: Transcriber / Translator
roles.description: Converts raw recordings into transcribed and translated text.

roles.name: Validator
roles.description: Checks transcriptions and translations for accuracy and fluency. Joins once collection begins.

roles.name: Super Reviewer
roles.description: Audits Validator output. Accountable for the dataset’s language purity. Independent: appointed by the government on a contract separate from the collection agency’s.
roles.example: E.g. a university linguist, a State Tribal Research Institute or a credentialed expert.

roles.name: Field Testers
roles.description: Briefed on the testing protocol and need not understand the model. Ask simple everyday questions and judge whether the system understands them and responds clearly.

roles.name: Engineering Teams
roles.description: Evaluate technical performance and analyse issues found in field testing.

roles.name: Subject Matter Experts
roles.description: Domain experts, for example in agriculture and health. Identified to review content, and they rate expert-evaluation queries for correctness, clarity, safety and local relevance.

roles.name: Independent Third Party
roles.description: Judges whether the deployed service is acceptable, standing apart from the vendor whose model is evaluated. Called the Independent Evaluator in the checklist.

phases.name: Readiness
phases.text: A “No” on any readiness item is a task to complete, not a disqualifier. Check which datasets already exist in the community before initiating the project. Foundation-building for one language spans roughly 6–9 months of active effort.

phases.name: Stage 0: Readiness and language confirmation
phases.text: Confirm the target language and an institutional anchor in writing, fill out the one-page Language Profile, and record the decision in an internal e-Office note. Done when the DC has confirmed the language and dialect starting point in writing.

phases.name: Stage 1: Team mobilisation and departmental order
phases.text: Nominate the Nodal Officer by post, set up one coordination channel, issue the departmental order that sets up the review mechanism, and begin identifying a Linguistic Expert, contributors and a Reviewer. Done when the order is issued and circulated and the Nodal Officer has begun onboarding the team.

phases.name: Stage 2: Community engagement and script and dialect decision
phases.text: The DC convenes the first community meeting in person, and three to four meetings are budgeted. Existing resources are collected and the Linguistic Expert makes the documented script and dialect call. Done when the decision is confirmed in writing and the first meeting is complete.

phases.name: Stage 3: Scope definition, vendor selection and work order
phases.text: Write the scope document with the technical specification, convert it into an RFP-equivalent, review proposals with the Steering Committee and sign the Work Order. Do not contract the vendor before the deployment owner and community leadership are in the room. Done when the Work Order is signed and the vendor’s work plan is cleared.

phases.name: Stage 4: Language survey
phases.text: Secondary research, mapping existing datasets and audio, field-verifying dialect boundaries, and a survey report. Settle script disputes first and do not run the survey alongside an open one. Done when the report is accepted and no script dispute remains.

phases.name: Stage 5: Standards creation
phases.text: Agree the orthography policy, annotation guidelines and metadata schema, and fix the quality bar against WER, BLEU and MOS. Slow institutional sign-off is the usual delay, so chase it directly. Done when the Technical Partner and Linguistic Expert have signed off the standards document.

phases.name: Stage 6: Pilot collection
phases.text: Register an initial contributor pool, take informed consent, collect a small trial batch, validate it and audit a sample. Do not compress the pilot to hit a date. Done when the Super Reviewer confirms the batch meets the quality bar and the Nodal Officer confirms the pool and protocol are ready to scale.

phases.name: Stage 7: Full collection, annotation and validation
phases.text: Record at scale, move data through the validation chain, track progress and quality separately every week, and run the weekly, fortnightly and monthly reviews. Each round: collect, transcribe, validate, fine-tune, test. The first keyword-spotting model should be shared in months 2–3. Done at Gate 1, when the Super Reviewer confirms the full dataset has passed the chain.

phases.name: Stage 8: Model building and benchmarking
phases.when: After Gate 1; about 1 week per fine-tuning cycle
phases.text: Train the models, benchmark them against WER, BLEU and MOS, feed collection gaps back, and fine-tune after every new round of data. Done at Gate 2, audited by the Quality PMU.

phases.name: Stage 9: Hosting and open release
phases.text: Receive the model and dataset, release both under CC BY 4.0 or equivalent, and confirm API and service availability. Done when hosting is live and the open licence is recorded.

phases.name: Stage 10: Application integration and field testing
phases.text: Integrate the model into the live service and run a field-testing phase with field testers, language experts and engineers. Done when issues are addressed, or deferred with a stated reason.

phases.name: Stage 11: Use-case acceptance and sign-off
phases.text: Run about a hundred real test interactions, ideally judged by an independent evaluator, and move to full deployment on a passed acceptance test. Done after two complete Gate 3 feedback cycles.

phases.name: Stage 12: Sustaining
phases.text: Write every non-delegable action into the departmental order, keep the dataset and model openly released, keep the playbook current, and continue the review cadence and quality checks. A project still dependent on its champion’s daily involvement has fallen short of done.

rules.rule: A committed deployment application before any data collection starts.
rules.why: The one non-negotiable gate. Models get trained and go unused otherwise.

rules.rule: Community leadership and the application owner in the room before a data collection vendor is contracted.
rules.why: Contracting collection first and looking for a deployment owner later is a documented failure.

rules.rule: Nominate the Nodal Officer before anything else is delegated.
Issue the review order in week one and lock the cadence from day one.
rules.why: A written order survives a transfer. A verbal agreement rarely does.

rules.rule: Bring validators in once collection formally starts.
rules.why: They become relevant at that point.

rules.rule: Review each work order with the Steering Committee before the next stage proceeds.
Integrate the application once, after the first model-building cycle.
rules.why: Later model updates flow through the same pipeline.

rules.rule: Insist on open data standards and ULCA-compatible exports from day one.
Check which datasets already exist in the community before initiating the project.
rules.why: Avoids collecting what is already there. The DC can check the community’s resources first.

rules.rule: Settle script disputes before starting the language survey.
rules.why: The survey commonly slips when a dispute carries over from the community meetings.

rules.rule: Budget three to four community meetings, and do not compress them or the pilot to hit a date.
rules.why: Rushed community trust-building is the single most common cause of later delay.

rules.rule: Hold a dedicated proposal walkthrough before finalising a vendor.
rules.why: Cost assumptions get checked, not accepted on trust.
